summary.text: A 9 year old male had a 10-day history of severe headache, vomiting, and numbness in the right arm and foot. Bilateral papilledema was found at the ophthalmic examination, and MRI displayed a mass in the left brain hemisphere and brainstem. After subtotal excision, histopathological examination led to a diagnosis of glioblastoma multiforme.

The excision was followed by cranial radiotherapy with a total dose of 60 Gy, then temozolomide and bevacizumab plus irinotecan as first and second-line treatments. Control MRI showed tumor progression despite these treatments, so nivolumab 3 mg/kg intravenously every two weeks was begun as third-line treatment.

Two days after the second dose, he was admitted with a rapidly progressive decline in visual acuity: counting fingers at 1 m in the right eye and light perception in the left, with bilateral optic disc swelling. Urgent MRI showed bilateral thickening of the optic nerves with normal intracranial pressure, and bilateral optic neuritis was diagnosed.

Nivolumab was stopped and intravenous corticosteroids (1 g/day) were given for 5 days, with progressive improvement in visual acuity. After a week the vision improved to 20/20 in both eyes, and no additional treatment was needed at the next follow-up.

ambiguities.issue: The abstract states the optic neuritis was induced by nivolumab and the conclusions call it an adverse event of nivolumab therapy, while the discussion says nivolumab is probably responsible.

evidence.quote: Herein, we describe the first report of a bilateral optic neuritis induced by nivolumab in a grade 4 glioblastoma multiforme patient.
Probably, nivolumab is responsible for the optic neuritis seen in this patient because of the short duration of time between nivolumab initiation and decrease in visual acuity in this case.
